description: External IDs are the foundational requirement for data migration and integration. Every object that participates in data loads must have an External ID field configured. External IDs serve three purposes: (1) upsert operations use them to match existing records, (2) relationship fields use them to establish parent-child links without knowing internal IDs, (3) integration patterns use them as the canonical cross-system identifier. Best practice: use a composite key pattern (SourceSystem_EntityType_SourceID) for global uniqueness.
setup_steps: Create External ID fields on ALL objects involved in data migration
Use indexed External ID fields for upsert performance
Establish naming convention: SourceSystem_EntityType_SourceID
Configure External ID uniqueness constraints (unique vs non-unique)
Map source system IDs to External ID fields in ETL
gotchas: External ID fields MUST be indexed for acceptable upsert performance at scale
Maximum 25 External ID fields per object (platform limit)
Non-unique External IDs will match the FIRST record found - can cause data corruption
Relationship fields referencing External IDs require the field to be on the parent object
Bulk API upserts with External IDs have different error handling than SOAP API
migration_relevance: Critical for any Veeva migration. Veeva External_ID_vod__c maps to custom External ID fields. Migration ETL MUST preserve external IDs for ongoing integration.

description: A Data Ownership Matrix defines which system is the master for each data domain. In life sciences deployments, typical ownership: MDM/ERP owns HCP/HCO master data, CRM owns interaction/activity data, compliance systems own consent data, marketing automation owns campaign data. The matrix must be defined BEFORE integration design. Conflicts arise when two systems claim ownership of the same field - resolve during design, not during go-live.
setup_steps: Identify all data domains (HCP, HCO, Product, Territory, Activity, Consent, Sample)
Map each domain to its system of record
Define field-level ownership where domain-level is insufficient
Document conflict resolution rules for each domain
Establish data stewardship roles
gotchas: Account/Contact master data is almost NEVER owned by CRM in life sciences - it comes from MDM or data vendors
Territory assignments typically flow FROM upstream systems, not from CRM
Sample inventory data has dual ownership: limits from compliance, transactions from CRM
Consent data ownership varies by jurisdiction - GDPR vs US requirements differ
migration_relevance: Veeva implementations often have unclear ownership boundaries. Migration is the opportunity to establish clean ownership. Document before migrating.

description: Four integration patterns for the platform: (1) Synchronous (REST/SOAP API) - for real-time single-record operations, (2) Asynchronous (Platform Events, Change Data Capture) - for event-driven near-real-time flows, (3) Batch (Bulk API, Data Loader) - for high-volume periodic loads, (4) UI-level (Canvas, iFrame, OmniScript) - for user-facing integration. Pattern selection depends on: volume (records/hour), latency requirement, data freshness requirement, and error handling complexity.
setup_steps: Classify each integration by volume, latency, and freshness requirements
Select appropriate pattern based on classification
Design error handling specific to the chosen pattern
Configure API limits and governor limit monitoring
Set up integration user accounts with appropriate permissions
gotchas: API call limits are per-org, not per-integration - multiple integrations share the same pool
Bulk API has a 15-minute processing window limit per batch
Platform Events have a 72-hour retention window - consumers must process within that window
Change Data Capture has a 3-day retention and does NOT capture all field changes (formula, rollup excluded)
Synchronous callouts from triggers have a 120-second timeout combined limit per transaction
migration_relevance: Veeva integration patterns may need redesign. Veeva custom middleware should be evaluated against native platform integration capabilities.

description: Seven anti-patterns from real implementations: (1) Flat structure - cramming all data into Account/Contact instead of using industry objects, (2) Over-customization - building custom objects that duplicate standard industry objects, (3) Picklist abuse - using picklists instead of junction objects for many-to-many relationships, (4) Missing External IDs - relying on Name matching instead of External IDs for upserts, (5) Trigger cascades - complex trigger chains that exceed governor limits, (6) Monolithic integration - one massive integration job instead of domain-specific integrations, (7) Ignoring sharing model - designing data access after the fact instead of during architecture.
setup_steps: Review current data model against industry standard objects
Identify custom objects that duplicate standard functionality
Audit relationships for picklist abuse
Verify External ID coverage on all integration-participating objects
Map trigger execution order and identify cascade risks
Design sharing model during architecture phase, not after
gotchas: Flat structure is the #1 migration anti-pattern - resist pressure to replicate legacy flat models
Over-customization creates long-term upgrade friction with platform releases
Trigger cascade failures are extremely hard to debug in production
Sharing model changes on large data volumes can take hours to recalculate
Monolithic integration jobs that fail require full restart - domain-specific jobs can be retried independently
migration_relevance: Most Veeva implementations have at least 2-3 of these anti-patterns. Migration is the opportunity to fix them - not replicate them.

description: Four strategies for handling data during migration: (1) Migrate-and-transform - move data with schema transformation to fit target model, (2) Migrate-as-is - direct field-to-field mapping for compatible schemas, (3) Archive-and-reference - move historical data to archive with reference links, (4) Rebuild - regenerate data from source systems rather than migrating from CRM. Strategy selection depends on data quality, volume, business value, and regulatory retention requirements.
setup_steps: Classify each data domain by migration strategy
Define data quality thresholds for each strategy
Configure archive storage for historical data
Set up data validation rules for migrated data
Plan rollback strategy for each migration phase
gotchas: Regulated data (samples, signatures, adverse events) may require migrate-and-transform for compliance
Archive-and-reference requires the archive to remain accessible for regulatory audits
Rebuild strategy is often underused - many data domains are better regenerated from source than migrated from CRM
Data quality issues in the source system will be amplified during transformation, not hidden
migration_relevance: Strategy selection is one of the highest-impact decisions in migration planning. Wrong strategy selection causes more migration failures than technical issues.

description: Platform scaling dimensions: (1) Data volume - large objects (10M+ records) need archiving strategy, (2) API volume - concurrent API calls have org-level limits, (3) User volume - sharing recalculation time grows with user count, (4) Integration volume - multiple concurrent integrations compete for API limits, (5) Storage - file storage and data storage are separately metered. Key thresholds: 200K+ records in a single object impacts query performance; 50M+ total records requires data archiving strategy; 10K+ users impacts sharing recalculation.
setup_steps: Profile current data volumes and growth projections
Identify objects approaching 200K record threshold
Configure data archiving for historical records
Set up API usage monitoring and alerting
Plan sharing model for projected user count
gotchas: Query performance degrades noticeably at 200K+ records without proper indexing
Sharing recalculation for 10K+ users can take hours - plan maintenance windows
File storage (attachments, documents) is often the first limit hit in life sciences (due to signatures, CLM content, documents)
Big objects and external objects can extend capacity but have limited query capabilities
migration_relevance: Veeva data volumes should be profiled before migration. Plan archiving strategy for historical data to avoid hitting platform limits on Day 1.

description: Three-layer security model: (1) Object-level security via profiles and permission sets - controls CRUD access per object, (2) Field-level security - controls visibility and editability per field per profile, (3) Record-level security via sharing rules, role hierarchy, and territory-based sharing. The platform supports User Mode for SOQL queries (enforces FLS and CRUD) and System Mode (bypasses security for internal operations). Industry-specific sharing: territory-based sharing aligns with sales territory alignment for record visibility.
setup_steps: Design role hierarchy aligned to organizational structure
Configure permission sets for each persona (sales, medical, compliance)
Set up territory-based sharing rules
Configure field-level security for sensitive fields (signatures, consent, samples)
Enable User Mode SOQL in all user-facing Apex code
Set up sharing rule recalculation monitoring
gotchas: With Sharing keyword in Apex is NOT the same as User Mode SOQL - they enforce different security layers
Territory-based sharing is separate from role hierarchy - both must be configured
Field-level security on relationship paths requires explicit FLS checks on each object in the path
Sharing rule recalculation after territory realignment can impact system performance
Permission set groups simplify assignment but still require individual permission set design
migration_relevance: Veeva security model must be mapped to platform security layers. Territory-based sharing is the closest equivalent to Veeva territory security.
